title: A first low-level drink-driving conviction reduced job entry for New Zealand workers
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: A first low-level drink-driving conviction reduced the likelihood of employment by an average 6.8 percentage points over the following two years in the New Zealand sample studied by Kabir Dasgupta and co-authors. That represented a 9.8% decline relative to employment in the month before conviction. The largest change was a reduced chance of starting work, particularly when the applicant had to form a new employment relationship. Monthly wage and salary earnings fell about NZ$90, or 2.3% relative to the earlier level. The outcome is relevant to how quickly people can return to work after a conviction. It is a much narrower estimate than the employment effect of criminal records in general (table 2).

The authors link court, tax and other administrative records for 1,824 New Zealand-born adults whose first conviction occurred during 2007–19. They restrict the sample to a single charge in a narrow band of measured alcohol levels and a standard sentence of a NZ$400–500 fine and 180 days’ licence suspension. They exclude people with a recorded accident in the month of the violation. These choices help separate labour-market effects from accident-related injury, variation in penalties or earlier criminal records. They also restrict generalization to other offences, migrants or people receiving more severe sanctions (section 3 and appendix table A.1).

The comparison uses the differing timing of convictions among people who eventually experience one. The event date is the last court hearing, when a conviction becomes visible, which can be later than the incident. The authors compare people already convicted with otherwise eligible people awaiting their own convictions. The design relies on similar trends in the absence of conviction and limited anticipation. The baseline outcomes display no clear divergence before treatment. An alternative comparison using closely matched people with no conviction gives similar patterns and somewhat smaller employment and entry effects. That comparison shows an earlier difference in job entry that largely closes before conviction (figure 3 and appendix C).

Entry among those initially out of work fell 8.2 percentage points, while exit among those initially employed rose 2.2 points. These are conditional rates with different denominators. The employment gap approached 15 points two years after the court date, well beyond the usual six-month suspension. In the more detailed accounting, moves to new employers in different industries and entry from non-employment explain almost the entire average employment loss. Pay for workers remaining with an employer or moving within the same narrowly defined industry changed little. Employment losses through new matches were larger in industries the authors classified as likely to screen applicants. They were also larger in industries that require relatively little driving, suggesting that temporarily losing a licence cannot account for the whole pattern (appendix tables B.2–B.5).

The authors interpret these findings through a hiring model. An employer unfamiliar with an applicant may treat a criminal record as information about reliability. Existing employers know more about a worker’s performance and have less reason to change a decision on that signal alone. Industry classifications proxy for likely checks and driving requirements. They do not observe an individual employer obtaining a record or rejecting a particular application. The study also finds differences in estimated effects across demographic groups, but cautions that several comparisons of their time paths are imprecise. It identifies a cost of the conviction for affected workers without measuring the road-safety benefits of enforcement or the net benefit of an alternative sentencing rule.

questions.question: At what point in hiring does a visible conviction reduce a worker’s chance of employment?
questions.detail: The paper finds fewer new matches in industries likely to screen applicants, but its administrative employment records cannot show a rejected application. Examine hiring-stage records, actual background-check requests and vacancy requirements, with suitable consent and confidentiality. Distinguish applications submitted, interviews, offers and acceptances. This would clarify whether recruitment practices or reduced applicant search explain the persistent entry gap.

questions.question: How much earnings risk comes from lost months of work versus lower pay in a subsequent job?
questions.detail: Average employment declines more sharply than monthly earnings among employed workers. Link payroll records to hours, employer changes and job start dates, and compare total earnings over common horizons across the affected and later-convicted groups. The distinction matters for household cash-flow stress and credit assessment, especially when a worker remains attached to an employer but later has to search again.

questions.question: Would a different treatment of low-level cases reduce employment costs while preserving safety?
questions.detail: The sample holds the sentence nearly constant and cannot identify how another disposal would perform. A focused evaluation could combine court assignment or diversion records, road-safety outcomes and linked tax data for comparably situated first-time defendants. Examine subsequent offending, injuries and employment together. Those comparisons are needed before turning a labour-market finding for a narrow group into an assessment of the economic costs and benefits of policy.
